ingredients.intro: The listing gives a Latin ingredient line of five plants, which is more than most jars on any shelf manage. It also gives a second list in prose, in common names, which runs to four of them and adds a proprietary blend. The two do not agree. Here are the five from the Latin line, which is the one we work from. We hold a photograph of one of the five, the damiana. The other four frames are empty, and any picture on this page that is a generated scene says so.

cards.p: A low cabbage-family plant grown on the Junin plateau in Peru, at altitudes above 4,000 metres where very little else is farmed. The part eaten and sold is the swollen underground storage organ, dried in the sun after lifting. The listing's prose calls it maca root, which makes it the one plant here whose part is printed.

A twining vine of damp woodland from the eastern United States down into Mexico, with heart-shaped leaves and a knotted underground rhizome. It is not the yam of the greengrocer, which is a different set of Dioscorea species grown as a staple food. This is the plant the listing's second list leaves out.

cards.fam: Fabaceae · the Mediterranean and western Asia
cards.p: An annual legume with small three-part leaves and hard angular yellow seed. The seed is the part usually sold, whole or ground, and it is the fenugreek of a curry powder and of the smell people describe as maple. Being a legume is the reason for the allergen note on the sheet below.

A tall umbellifer with hair-fine leaves and flat yellow flower heads, native to the Mediterranean and naturalised on roadsides across much of the world. Both the seed and the swollen leaf base are used in kitchens. Which part is in this jar is not printed.

cards.alt: A small damiana shrub with toothed leaves and a yellow flower
cards.p: A small aromatic shrub of Mexico, Central America and the West Indies, with toothed leaves and small yellow flowers. The leaf is the part usually dried and sold. Older books file the genus in a family of its own, Turneraceae, which has since been folded into Passifloraceae.

cards.common: Five names against four and a blend
cards.p: The Latin ingredient line names five plants and no blend. The paragraph underneath names four of them in English, drops wild yam, and adds a proprietary blend that the Latin line does not mention. One of those two lists is out of date and we cannot tell you which. The Latin line is the one this page works from, and the mismatch is printed here rather than tidied away.

rows: Five botanicals, named in Latin on the listing's ingredient line.

Anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding, which is the listing's own caution. Not for children. Fenugreek is a legume, in the same family as peanut and chickpea, and people who react to those sometimes react to it. Fennel belongs to the carrot and celery family, which is another well known allergen group. If you take any prescribed medicine, speak to your GP or pharmacist before you start. The listing also asks anyone undergoing hormone therapy to speak to a healthcare professional before use, and that stays on this page.
spec.smallprint: Do not exceed the stated dose. Speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, particularly if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or take medication. Food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a varied and balanced diet and a healthy lifestyle. Keep out of reach of young children.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: Five plants are named here in Latin, the milligrams, the count, the serving and the day rate are all printed, and where the listing carries two lists that disagree, both are on this page. Feminina is the name on the jar. It is a name, not a description, and we do not expand it. What any of these plants does in a body is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: Two lists, and neither of them is wrong on purpose
paras: This listing does something almost no jar on any shelf does: it names five plants in Latin, on the ingredient line, before it says anything else. That line is the reason this page exists in the shape it does. You can take any one of those five names, look it up in a flora, and check it.

Then, four paragraphs down, there is a second list in English that names four of the five and adds a proprietary blend. Wild yam has gone. I do not know which of the two lists came first, and I am not going to guess in public, so both are on the sheet with the disagreement marked.

The fix is a printing job rather than a reformulation, and it is on the list for the next label. Until then, the Latin line is what this page works from, because a binomial is checkable and an English name is a nickname.

The fenugreek note on the sheet is the one thing on this page I would not want anybody to skip. It is a legume, in with peanut and chickpea, and that matters to some people regardless of anything else.
reiss.pull: A binomial is checkable. An English name is a nickname.
